title: At my table (2 Samuel 9)
hookLine: David seeks Jonathan's lame son and seats him at his table always

lines: IS ANYONE LEFT OF SAUL'S HOUSE?
cards: A question, asked in a palace: is there anyone still left of the house of Saul, so I can show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? David is settled now, with a city and an army.
A new king asking after the old king's family could sound like a threat.

But David is remembering a field, and arrows, and an oath Jonathan made him swear: the Lord between me and you, between my children and your children. Someone remembers a name, a servant of Saul's house called Ziba.

teach.h: A SON OF JONATHAN, LAME IN HIS FEET.
teach.b: Ziba says yes. There's a son of Jonathan, lame in his feet, living in someone else's house in a place called Lo-debar. His name is Mephibosheth.

Earlier the book told how it happened: he was a small child when news came of the battle where his father and grandfather died, and his nurse snatched him up and ran, and he fell. David sends for him.
Mephibosheth comes in and falls on his face, with every reason to be afraid. David says his name. Here is your servant, he answers.
Then David tells him: fear not. I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father's sake. I'll give you back all the land of Saul, and you will eat bread at my table continually.
The Hebrew for kindness here is chesed, loyal love, the faithfulness you owe because of a bond. When David first asked Ziba, he even called it the kindness of God.
Mephibosheth can hardly take it in; he calls himself a dead dog. David doesn't argue. He just keeps the promise.
Ziba's household will work the land, and Mephibosheth will eat at the king's table like one of the king's sons.
The chapter ends with two facts side by side: he ate always at the king's table, and he was lame in both his feet.

teach.h: LIKE ONE OF THE KING'S SONS.
teach.b: Nothing about him had to change to get a seat. The table changed. David kept faith with a friend who was gone by keeping a place for his son.

how: Jews read the story of Mephibosheth in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, as an example of chesed, loyal kindness, kept across generations.

o: loyal love, the faithfulness owed to a bond
charity given to strangers who ask for it
a king's pardon for his enemy's family

games.q: at my table — tap the pairs.
p: Jonathan's son, lame in his feet
loyal love, kindness owed to a bond

s: David looked for Saul's heirs to remove them
he asked so he could show kindness for Jonathan's sake.
David told the frightened Mephibosheth to fear not
he said his name, then fear not, then promised him Saul's land and a seat at his table.
Mephibosheth was healed before he sat at the table
the chapter ends: he ate always at the king's table, and was lame in both his feet.

games.q: you're David, now king. you learn that Jonathan's son is alive, lame, and living in someone else's house. what do you do?
o: leave him alone: he's safer forgotten.
send him money and keep your distance.
bring him in, give back his land, and seat him at your table.
games.why: David says fear not, restores all of Saul's land to him, and seats him at the king's table like one of the king's sons.

practice: Let one friend come to mind who has died, moved far away, or drifted out of touch, and think of the people they left behind: a partner, a child, a parent.
Ask what a seat at your table would look like for one of them: a dinner, a message on the anniversary, a story about their person they haven't heard. If you pray, you can hold their names.

wordCard.voice: chesed. The loyal love David showed Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, giving him land back and a permanent seat at the king's table. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: at my table, from David's promise in 2 Samuel 9:7.

carryVoice: Your line: always at my table. A promise kept for someone who's gone. Day seven hundred forty-five, done.
